transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-10-29 15:00 PT
Duration: 47 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Luis (Redwood SE), Arun (CTO), Sofia (SRE), Jacob (PM)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): Customer cares about how Redwood handles partial degradation and what 'acceptable' error rate looks like under simulated region outages. They want artifacts for compliance and a concrete pilot.

Topics: fallback policies, multi-region routing, chaos test plan, SLA/deg-rate acceptance, hosted vs dedicated vs private, telemetry required for pilot

Action items (outlined during call): see metadata list above

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — appreciate you making time. I'm Maya from Redwood Inference, AE on this account, and with me is Luis, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Arun: Good, thanks. Running late morning here. Sofia's in SRE land so she may jump in with infra stuff.
[00:13] Sofia: Yep, hi, apologies if I get a bit technical.
[00:16] Jacob: Morning all. We're mainly trying to validate an operational tolerance number — how much degradation we accept when a region or capacity tier goes noisy.
[00:24] Luis: Great, thanks. Quick agenda — understand your current infra and SLOs, walk through fallback options (hosted/dedicated/private), and talk pilot/chaos test approach. Does that sound OK?
[00:32] Arun: Yes. We run inference for multimodal assistant at 600 qps peaks with spikes to 1.2k during campaigns. We care about 95th/99th latency and also steady throughput — and in a failure we'd accept some degradation but need to quantify it.
[00:45] Sofia: Right. We ran two internal fires earlier this year and saw latency tails flip badly when cache misses and model swaps happen. We want to capture that with a repeatable chaos sim.
[00:55] Maya: When you say 'degradation', do you mean higher latency, higher error rate, or request drops?
[01:01] Arun: All of the above really. But product level, Jacob wants to know acceptable drop in successful responses — say we can tolerate X% increase in 95th latency and Y% request drop.
[01:12] Jacob: The product team will accept up to a roughly 15% increase in 95th latency for short windows, but request drop should be under 2% overall. Those are starting numbers.
[01:23] Luis: OK, that's helpful. On Redwood side we have three levers: config routing (region steering + pinning), model variants and fallback (e.g., move to a lower capacity model or quantized variant), and capacity tiers (dedicated reserved pools with burst vs hosted shared pools).
[01:37] Sofia: Can you explain how 'fallback' happens automatically? I'm worried about noisy neighbor scenarios where one GPU gets starved and we end up with a thundering herd on fallback.
[01:48] Luis: Good question. Briefly, fallback is policy-driven. You can set thresholds by latency, error, or capacity signals. When threshold hit, smart-routing will steer new requests to healthy regions or model variants. Also we support soft-fallback where a percentage of traffic shifts for validation before full cutover. There is also circuit-breaker style backoff to avoid thundering herds.
[02:08] Arun: Does that mean the KV cache gets invalidated and causes a cold start everywhere? Our prefix cache is big; we rely on prefix cache for latency.
[02:16] Luis: We try not to invalidate caches globally. Prefix/KV caches are local to serving nodes. When we reroute we warm caches via staged traffic or warmup preloads. For chaos tests we can simulate cache loss to measure worst-case.
[02:31] Maya: Jumping in — we're hearing you want an acceptance criteria based on chaos tests. We typically run a pilot: traffic replay from a recent 72-hour window, then inject failure modes (region outage, GPU throttling, cache flush) and measure delta on 95/99 and success-rate.
[02:45] Jacob: How long does that pilot usually take? We need it in the next 3 weeks ideally.
[02:51] Luis: A minimal pilot can be 1 week: 2 days setup & data ingest, 2 days of controlled runs, and 1 day of analysis and report. If you want Hosted + Dedicated comparison, add a week.
[03:03] Sofia: For Dedicated does Redwood give us reserved pools? We want to avoid noisy neighbor but also need predictable costs.
[03:10] Luis: Yes, Dedicated pools are reserved GPU capacity for your account. They give predictable throughput and isolation. For noisy neighbor, Dedicated is the best mitigation vs Hosted shared tenancy. Private deployment gives max control but requires on-prem/VPC fiddling.
[03:24] Arun: What's the tradeoff on latency between Hosted and Dedicated? I assume Dedicated is better because of isolation?
[03:29] Luis: Typically Dedicated has lower tail latency since you avoid noisy neighbors and can pick instance types or quantization profiles optimized for your model. But Hosted can be tuned, and for many customers the difference is small if you use reserved burst and smart routing.
[03:42] Jacob: Can Redwood do region steering at request level? For example, send write-ish operations to region A, and read-ish to region B, or a geo-based policy?
[03:50] Maya: Yes. We have routing policies based on customer-defined rules, latency SLOs, and failover. You can pin model version + region per route.
[03:57] Sofia: Sounds good. About SLAs — do you offer financial SLAs for Hosted or only Dedicated?
[04:03] Maya: We have SLA-backed commitments for Dedicated and enterprise Private contracts. Hosted has strong uptime targets but historically isn't offered as a financial-backed SLA unless you commit to an enterprise plan.
[04:15] Arun: For compliance, we need audit logs and KMS integration if we do Private. Can you surface the audit trails during chaos runs? We need to tie events to user operations.
[04:25] Luis: Audit logs and KMS/HSM integrations are available for Private and Dedicated. Hosted also supports some audit logging and key management integrations, but Private gives you the most control. We can include detailed telemetry from the pilot—request traces, token-level latencies, model variant switches, and routing decisions.
[04:41] Jacob: For the chaos sim, what's your recommended acceptance metric? We talked about 15% 95th and under 2% drops, but do you usually formalize that?
[04:51] Luis: We recommend two tiers: tolerance (short transient spikes acceptable for up to T minutes) and recovery (how quickly you bounce back). For example, accept up to 15% 95th latency increase sustained no more than 10 minutes, and total dropped requests under 2% averaged over a 1-hour window. We can codify these in the pilot report.
[05:09] Sofia: And what about fallbacks that change model quality? If you downgrade to a quantized model, do you provide quality regression checks? Our product owners will push back if hallucination rates go up.
[05:20] Luis: We tie quality monitors to prompt sets and key evals. For fallbacks that change model or quantization, we run a preconfigured eval set and report any regressions. We can also set auto-rollbacks if quality crosses thresholds.
[05:33] Arun: How do you route when a region is flapping? We can't have constant re-routing causing more instability.
[05:40] Luis: We have hysteresis and cooldown windows on routing decisions. Also staged ramping: move 10% for 30s, validate, then 50%, etc. That avoids oscillation. There's also a failback policy if latency improves.
[05:53] Jacob: Any known blind spots we should be aware of?
[05:56] Luis: One is KV cache locality — big caches are expensive to warm across regions, so worst-case cold path latency can be substantially higher. Also if you're using stateful session caches we need to plan how to rebuild them.
[06:08] Sofia: For our tests I'd like the pilot to include a cache-warmup plan and then a full flush test as worst-case. Also show how fast cache warms with traffic replay.
[06:18] Luis: Noted. We'll include both warm and cold path tests.
[06:21] Maya: Switching to compliance — you'll want SOC 2 docs, and if Private we provide a deployment checklist. We'll share the SOC 2 and network architecture whitepaper after this call.
[06:31] Arun: Perfect. On instrumentation, what telemetry do you need from us to run realistic traffic replay?
[06:36] Luis: Ideally recent 72-hour traces with timestamps, request types, average token lengths, and contextual groups. If you can't share raw data, synthetic but shaped traces work. We also need a mapping of request routes to model versions.
[06:49] Jacob: We can export anonymized traces. Is there a required format?
[06:52] Luis: CSV or parquet with columns for timestamp, route, prompt_token_count, response_token_count, success/fail flag. We'll supply a template.
[06:59] Sofia: About network topology — if we do Private in our VPC, how does Redwood manage the control plane? We want the control plane out-of-band but the data path in our VPC.
[07:08] Maya: That's exactly the model: private control plane (Redwood-managed but no data plane access), and the inference data plane lives in your VPC or on-prem. We'll provide the deployment guide.
[07:18] Arun: Ok, cost: if we run chaos sims against Hosted versus Dedicated, do you estimate compute cost?
[07:23] Luis: Yes, we'll include a cost comparison in the pilot proposal — token costs, reserved capacity amortization, and expected additional egress or warmup cost.
[07:31] Jacob: Quick question — during fallback to lower-capacity models, do you preserve prompt enrichment features or function-calling hooks? We don't want a regression in function behavior.
[07:41] Luis: Good call. We preserve protocol-level features like function-calling and structured output, but model-specific behavior can change. We'll surface any functional mismatches in the report.
[07:52] Sofia: For the chaos injection itself, do you run chaos in prod or an isolated staging environment?
[07:58] Luis: We strongly recommend staging with production-like traffic replays. If you want to run in prod we require strict safeties and rollbacks; most customers start in staging.
[08:08] Arun: We're leaning towards staging for initial tests.
[08:11] Maya: Good. We'll propose a staged pilot and include a Hosted vs Dedicated comparison.
[08:17] Jacob: Anything else on SLOs? We also want to test multi-region partial loss, where region B loses 60% capacity for 15 minutes.
[08:27] Luis: We'll include a scenario matrix: full region outage, partial capacity loss, disk/IO throttling on hosts, and cache flush. For each we'll measure 95/99 latency, error rate, and time-to-stable routing.
[08:41] Sofia: And we'd like the artifact to show for each scenario the routing decision timeline and the metric deltas.
[08:46] Luis: Yup, that's standard. We'll provide per-route timelines, token-level latencies, and a narrative.
[08:54] Arun: On a related note, how quickly can Redwood scale additional capacity if we see sustained traffic? We're worried about cold provisioning taking minutes and compounding latency.
[09:03] Luis: Autoscaling is configured per-pool. With warm pools you can have seconds-to-sub-minute capacity via burst; cold scale for new GPU instances can be minutes. For critical paths we suggest reserved capacity or pre-warmed burst.
[09:16] Jacob: Pre-warmed burst sounds right for our campaigns.
[09:19] Maya: We'll include configuration recommendations — how much reserved vs burst based on your traffic shapes.
[09:25] Sofia: For the pilot, can you simulate noisy neighbors — like artificially limiting GPU bandwidth?
[09:31] Luis: Yes, we can throttle I/O or inject latency at the host level in staging. That helps validate fallback thresholds.
[09:38] Arun: How do we ensure consistent test environments across Hosted and Dedicated to make the comparison fair?
[09:43] Luis: We'll standardize on the same request replay, model version, and sequence-length distributions. Where possible, pick matching instance types for Dedicated to approximate Hosted hardware. We'll note unavoidable differences.
[09:56] Jacob: Any limitations on our side to run the pilot — network peering, consent?
[10:00] Maya: We'll need an infra contact to arrange peering or data ingestion, and a legal PO for pilot terms. Those are usual.
[10:08] Sofia: I can be infra contact. I'll also share SLOs and traces.
[10:12] Arun: Timeline — can we get a pilot proposal by next Monday? That gives us time to align procurement.
[10:19] Maya: We can. Luis, can you put together the test matrix + pricing?
[10:23] Luis: Yes, I'll draft it and include a quick-run and full-run option.
[10:28] Jacob: On quality checks, can Redwood integrate our existing eval harness? We have internal eval scripts that compute hallucination and rouge-like metrics.
[10:36] Luis: We can either ingest your eval harness or export model outputs for you to run. If you want integrated reporting we'll pipe outputs through your eval harness during pilot.
[10:46] Sofia: That would be ideal.
[10:48] Maya: Noted. We'll propose integrated and non-integrated options.
[10:52] Arun: Any security red flags we should expect?
[10:55] Luis: Nothing out of the ordinary — if you do Private you'll own keys and network boundaries, Dedicated requires IP allowlists and VPN/peering. We'll share our security checklist.
[11:05] Jacob: Can you give an example of a fallback policy DSL or config? Our ops folks want concrete examples.
[11:12] Luis: Sure — a policy can be: if route.latency_95th > 1.5x baseline for 90s AND error_rate > 0.5% then shift 30% traffic to fallback_model for 60s, validate quality, then ramp to 100% if OK. We'll include a few templates.
[11:30] Sofia: That helps.
[11:33] Maya: We're about 40 minutes in — any final questions before we wrap?
[11:38] Arun: One last: will performing the pilot on Hosted risk data residency concerns? Our data residency requirements are strict for PII.
[11:45] Luis: If PII is a concern we recommend Dedicated or Private. Hosted can be configured with region pinning, but for strict residency we suggest Private and we can do an on-prem deployment.
[11:56] Jacob: Ok that's clear.
[11:58] Maya: Recap of next steps: we'll send pilot proposal and pricing, SOC 2 & deployment guide, and a chaos test plan. Luis will draft the matrix and test templates. Sofia will provide traces and SLOs. We'll aim to kick off pilot the week of 2026-11-03.
[12:15] Arun: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[12:18] Sofia: Thanks.
[12:20] Luis: Thanks all. We'll follow up with links and the CSV template for traces.
[12:25] Maya: End call.
